name: Maya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at the gold mine, the huge digger that loads the haul trucks. Each bucket is about 50 tonnes of rock, and four passes fill a truck, so a lot of my day is about timing: swing, dump, back to the face, while the next truck backs in. I'm in the cab by 6:30 after the pre-start, and if the trucks are flowing it's a good shift. I'm average at it, honestly, I'm steady but I'm not the fastest loader on the crew.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm, when it all clicks. What wears me out is the uncertainty at home. My husband Dan is a sparky, an electrician, on contract work, so some months he's flat out and some months he's got nothing. With Ella, who's 15, and Noah, who's 12, and the mortgage, we never get ahead. I'm on the lower end of the pay scale here because I took a lower-paid role to get days instead of nights while the kids were small. I'm also in the volunteer fire brigade, which is the one thing I do just for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds about right. Every new thing gets oversold, then it settles down into something useful. I'd probably say that over a barbecue, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. Not because I'm against it, but because I don't have the money to ride out a big change right now. A quiet few years would let us catch up a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and finally set up an automatic transfer into savings, even if it's only $50 a week. I'd keep using the AI app now and then for things like the brigade's rosters. And I'd push Dan to look for a steady job instead of contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Like a long weekend when nothing's due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the AI app for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small things. The brigade captain asked me to sort out the training roster, and the app turned my messy notes into a proper table. Ella showed me how. I don't use it every day, but it's handy when it saves me an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push Dan toward a steady job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when his work dries up, we live on my pay, and my pay doesn't stretch. Last March he had six weeks with nothing and we put the groceries on the credit card. I don't want to do that again.

S0.say: She'd say it sounds about right, since every new thing is oversold then settles into something useful. She'd say it over a barbecue rather than online.
S0.think: She'd be relieved, not out of opposition to AI but because the family can't afford to ride out big change right now. A quiet few years would let them catch up.
S0.do: Carries on and sets up an automatic $50 a week transfer into savings. Keeps using an AI app now and then for brigade rosters and pushes her husband to find steady work instead of contracts.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a long weekend with nothing due.
S0.quote: Last March he had six weeks with nothing and we put the groceries on the credit card.
S0.fieldNote: Her relief is about money and timing, not dislike of technology. She uses AI for small jobs once someone has shown her how, which fits her steady style. The household's real weak point is her husband's irregular contract work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fair warning and people should get ready, not panic. Some of the jobs on site will change and some will go, and the company and the government both need to help with that. I'd say that at work if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think shovel operators last longer than truck drivers, because loading is fiddly and every face is different. But not forever. I'd want to be moving before I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw a couple of people at the mine make the switch and it worked for them, I'd go for the same thing, probably remote operations or something in maintenance planning. In the first year I'd do one short course the company offers and build savings to a month. We'd cut the second streaming service and the gym membership I barely use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I'd feel like I had a bit of time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for a couple of people to make the switch first. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people jump at the first new thing and regret it. When they brought in a new rostering system, two of the girls moved to the planning office and it got cut a year later. I'd want to see that the new job actually lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shovel partner on the other shift, Kev, he's 60 and he's been loading trucks since before I was born. He'd hate a desk. And Dan, if the new mine gear needs fewer sparkies on contract.

S1.say: She'd say it's a fair warning to get ready, not panic, and that the company and government both need to help. She'd say it at work if asked.
S1.think: She thinks shovel operators last longer than truck drivers because every dig face is different, but not forever. She wants to move before she's forced.
S1.do: Waits until a couple of colleagues have switched successfully, then follows into remote operations or maintenance planning. Does one company short course in the first year, builds savings to a month and cuts a streaming service and gym membership.
S1.feel: Uneasy but steady, with a sense of having some time.
S1.quote: Two of the girls moved to the planning office and it got cut a year later.
S1.fieldNote: Her caution comes from watching colleagues jump too early and lose out. She is planning a measured move rather than resisting or rushing. She worries about both her shift partner and her husband's contract work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a sensible plan, fast, and less shouting. Government should keep people's incomes going for a while, and companies that save millions should chip in. I'd try to be the calm voice in the brigade group chat, because people would be frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. If AI can run the shovel and the remote room, my whole careful plan doesn't matter. And if Dan's contracts dry up at the same time, we've got about three weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd take every course the company offers anyway, because it might keep me on for the last stretch. I'd sit down with Dan and the bank about the mortgage before we're behind, and we'd cut everything we can, including Ella's guitar lessons. Once it arrived, I'd apply for whatever support there was and lean on Dan's parents, who own their place outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened and a bit stunned. I'd be doing the sums every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not enough to retrain properly, but enough to get the house in order. Talk to the bank, sell the camper, build a bit of a buffer. It's more about softening the landing than changing direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ella, who's 15?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, because she'd find out anyway on her phone. I'd say we're going to be careful for a while and she might have to work a part-time job. She'd be fine, she's tougher than me.

S2.say: She'd call for a sensible plan fast with less shouting: government keeping incomes going and companies chipping in. She'd try to be a calm voice in the brigade chat.
S2.think: She'd be scared because AI running both the shovel and the remote room makes her careful plan pointless. If her husband's contracts dry up too, they have about three weeks of money.
S2.do: Takes every company course in the two years before, talks to the bank about the mortgage early and cuts spending including guitar lessons and the camper. Once it arrives, applies for support and leans on her in-laws.
S2.feel: Frightened and stunned, doing sums every night.
S2.quote: It's more about softening the landing than changing direction.
S2.fieldNote: She keeps her centrist calm in public while being privately scared. With two years she shifts from career planning to protecting the household. Her in-laws owning their home outright is the family's real safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, if people start now. I'd tell the younger ones at the mine not to wait. And I'd want the government to fund retraining properly, with some help from the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years is enough for me to make one solid move. Not into mining, though, because that's going. Maybe something in emergency services, which I already know from the brigade, if that's still people-run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do my first-aid and fire certificates to a higher level, using the AI app to study. I'd watch for a year whether paid fire and rescue jobs are holding up in this picture, then apply. We'd also aim for two months of savings by year three, with Dan's help if his work holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Like a fire season where you know it's coming and you prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait a year to see if fire jobs hold up. Isn't that cutting it close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'd rather lose a year than switch into something that's gone by 2031. That's just how I am. I'd do the study in the meantime, so I'm ready either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the mortgage in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd try to get it down a bit, or at least not take on anything new. We were going to redo the kitchen. That's off.

S3.say: She'd say five years is tight but workable if people start now, and urge younger miners not to wait. She'd want government-funded retraining with company help.
S3.think: Five years is enough for one solid move, away from mining. She's thinking of emergency services, which she knows from the brigade, if those stay people-run.
S3.do: Upgrades her first-aid and fire certificates in year one with AI help, watches for a year whether paid fire and rescue jobs hold up, then applies. Aims for two months of savings by year three and cancels the kitchen renovation.
S3.feel: Anxious in a workable way, like preparing for a fire season.
S3.quote: I'd rather lose a year than switch into something that's gone by 2031.
S3.fieldNote: Her volunteer brigade work gives her a natural second path, which she only named once there was time. She still builds in a year of watching before committing, true to her steady style. She studies in the meantime so the wait isn't wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this sensibly, and we should stop arguing about whether it's coming and start planning. Schools, councils, the mine, all of them. I'd say it at a town meeting if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels okay for me personally. I'd be 53, the kids would be through school, and I could make a move in my own time. It's money that still worries me, not skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the shovel for the first few years and save, then move into fire and rescue or something like it around year four or five, once I'm sure it lasts. I'd help Ella and Noah choose study paths with the future in mind. And I'd try to get to three months of savings, which we've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with some worry underneath. It feels like a long project rather than an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noah, who's 12?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He loves anything with engines. I'd tell him to learn how the new machines work, not just how to drive them. The people who fix things always seem to have work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point where you'd stop waiting and just move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the company starts trialling self-driving shovels at our pit. That's my line. Once I see one at our mine, I go.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough to plan sensibly, and that schools, councils and the mine should stop arguing and start. She'd say it at a town meeting.
S4.think: Ten years feels okay: at 53 with kids through school, she could move in her own time. Money, not skills, still worries her.
S4.do: Stays on the shovel and saves for the first years, then moves into fire and rescue around year four or five, or as soon as self-driving shovels are trialled at her pit. Guides her children's study choices and aims for three months of savings.
S4.feel: Fairly calm with worry underneath, more a long project than an emergency.
S4.quote: When the company starts trialling self-driving shovels at our pit. That's my line. Once I see one at our mine, I go.
S4.fieldNote: She has a clear trigger for acting, which fits her wait-for-proof style. The extra time lets her plan around her kids finishing school. Money remains her one steady fear across every picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I couldn't learn something new, but because we'd run out of money before I got the chance. What would help is income support that bridges the gap for a year or so, and paid training places, so you're not choosing between a course and the groceries.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the volunteers. Half the fire brigade here are miners. If the mine goes and people move away, who turns up when there's a bushfire? Nobody's thinking about that.

headlineQuote: Half the fire brigade here are miners. If the mine goes and people move away, who turns up when there's a bushfire?
portrait: Maya Baker is a 43-year-old rope shovel operator at a gold mine, married to a contract electrician whose work comes and goes, with two teenagers and almost no savings. She is a calm, practical centrist who wants both government and companies to help, and her habit is to wait until a change is proven before moving. Her volunteer fire brigade work becomes her second path once there's enough time. In the two-year AGI picture, her careful plans give way to protecting the household and leaning on her in-laws.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because the family would run out of money before she had the chance to learn something new.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that bridges the gap for a year or so, and paid training places so people don't have to choose between a course and groceries.
